_comment: Drafted replies keyed by tweet id. Edit freely; the review page reads these as starting text and sends whatever is in the box.

replies.2039527567204704560: Ferrofluid separation is genuinely clever. The bar it has to clear is that reverse osmosis already removes microplastics along with PFAS, lead and fluoride, so the interesting question is cost and throughput rather than capability.
replies.2029338367943688702: The clip leans on skin contact, but inhalation is probably the bigger route. Those fibres end up in indoor air and house dust, which is why exposure carries on long after the leggings come off.
replies.2060403042084933833: Clearest write up of this I have seen. The thing that will still get lost downstream is that binding plastic inside the gut is not the same as clearing what is already lodged in tissue. Those get reported as one finding.
replies.2060152157739913412: Worth one caveat: that study tested a single isolated strain, Leuconostoc mesenteroides CBA3656, in germ free mice, not kimchi the food. It bound about 87 percent of polystyrene nanoplastics in a dish, which is a long way from eating kimchi.
replies.2033255150152794289: Billions per cup, and the fix is unusually cheap. Loose leaf with a steel infuser takes plastic out of the brewing path entirely, no special product required.
replies.2034572325039792277: The part that makes it hard to act on is the label. All of that hides behind one ingredient line reading gum base, and none of the polymers have to be named. Chicle based brands are the only reliable way out.
replies.2003215719987589611: The route people miss is that it does not stay outdoors. Tire particles are a measurable share of roadside air and settled house dust, so this is an inhalation story too, not only a waterways and food chain one.
replies.1744799330241048854: Your closing question is the interesting one. Tap is usually the better bet, but mostly after filtration, since municipal testing does not cover nano either. Unfiltered tap can just swap one unmeasured thing for another.
replies.1894146042473357355: Reverse osmosis is the right call. It is the only household technology that removes PFAS, microplastics, lead and fluoride together. Everything else covers a subset, which is fine once you know which subset you actually need.
replies.2061886419828678853: No human study shows fibre removes plastic particles already in your tissues. The kernel of truth is narrower: some fibre research shows lower BPA, which is a chemical rather than a particle. That swap is the most common trick in this whole category.
replies.1995176669749919806: The bit people stall on is what to replace it with. Borosilicate and tempered soda lime glass are both genuinely microwave safe. The trap is buying a glass container that still ships with a plastic lid.
replies.1920131611112427935: The size distinction matters more than most coverage admits. Nanoplastics are the fraction that crosses membranes, and certification has not caught up to them. NSF 401 covers microplastics, with no equivalent for nano.
replies.2025564201230504065: Worth adding that the 700,000 figure is per wash, and fleece also sheds while worn, which no laundry fix touches. Cut pile leaves far more loose fibre ends than a woven synthetic, so fleece is the worst case rather than the average.
replies.2052466542445805988: The claim that would make this checkable is the detection limit and the contamination controls. Michigan researchers just found nitrile and latex gloves alone can add thousands of false positives per square millimetre. Zero is a measurement claim before it is a biological one.
replies.2054584955162796069: Worth separating which findings this touches. It hits counts that leaned on infrared and Raman spectra. It does not obviously touch detections confirmed by other methods, and conflating the two is how this becomes microplastics were a hoax by Thursday.
replies.2037137492164399504: The measurement here is particles in waste, which is not the same as removal from tissue. Unabsorbed particles pass through and show up in stool whether or not anything bound them. Tissue burden before and after is the study that would settle it.
replies.2073678265424719887: The UCLA work put it at hundreds to thousands of fragments per piece. What makes it hard to avoid is the label: the polymer hides behind one ingredient line reading gum base. Chicle based brands are the way out of it.
replies.2032837865026077152: Encouraging, and worth pairing with what already works at home. Reverse osmosis removes microplastics today, alongside PFAS, lead and fluoride. Prototypes matter for scale. They do not change what you can do this week.
replies.1674553909032136704: Those numbers are exactly why microwave safe is such a misleading label. It is a melting standard. It means the container will not warp, and says nothing about what heat drives out of it. Borosilicate glass sidesteps the question entirely.
replies.1581344421752160257: The exposure route worth adding is inhalation. Synthetic textiles and house dust put particles into indoor air, and for infants floor level air is a much bigger share of the day than it is for the rest of us.
replies.1882502997390893238: The flame retardant finding is the part that surprised people. Worth knowing it was not only takeout containers. Black plastic kitchen utensils turned up in the same testing, and those sit directly in hot pans.
replies.1990460849874436393: The finding that actually moved things is detection in human tissue: blood, placenta, brain. What is still genuinely unsettled is dose response. We know the particles are there. We do not yet know how much of it matters.
replies.1849921149964255540: The awkward part is that a filter bag or a cooler wash only touches the wastewater share. Nothing in the laundry routine reduces what sheds while the garment is worn, so fabric choice is the only lever on that half.
replies.2061839263423951292: Good to see plastic already on that list, most fertility guides skip it. One gap worth closing: supplement capsules are their own exposure route, which matters when the same list recommends fish oil and a multivitamin.
